digo: Mnyumbu; Mchumbu (var. Mnyumbu madzi / Mchumbu madzi)
digo_source: Pakia (2005) App. III; Pakia (2005) App. VI; Maundu & Tengnäs 2005

teaser.en: Its inner bark becomes string and baskets, its fruit is a snack, and its trunk becomes mortars and beehives.

summary.en: *Mnyumbu*, the false marula, is a deciduous tree of wooded grassland and river valleys with flaking bark and small red-purple fruits. Almost every part is put to use, from string and dye to mortars, stools and medicine.

about.en:
*Mnyumbu* is a deciduous tree up to 20 metres tall with grey-brown bark that flakes off. The leaves are made of a few shiny leaflets, crowded at the ends of the branches. The fruits are small and red-purple.

It looks something like its cousin the marula, *mng'ongo*, which is why it is called the false marula.

where.en: It grows in wooded grassland, dry forest and river valleys.

uses.en:
The inner bark is stripped for string and woven into baskets, and the bark also gives a brown dye. The fruit is edible.

The wood is carved into mortars, stools and beehives. The bark and roots are used in traditional medicine.

names.en: Pakia records two Digo names, *mnyumbu* and *mchumbu*, and notes that they are interchangeable. Each has a variety with *madzi*, 'water', added: *mnyumbu madzi* and *mchumbu madzi*. The Giriama name is *mjumbu maji*. In Swahili it is *mnyumbu* or *mongo*; *mongo* is also used for the true marula.

reason.en: The true marula, a close relative
Wild fruit tree of the same family
Another member of the cashew family
Also used for bark string and mats

sources: Pakia, M. (2005) African Traditional Plant Knowledge Today: an ethnobotanical study of the Digo at the Kenya Coast. PhD thesis, Univ. Bayreuth, Appendix III (Digo–botanical name list) & Appendix VI (name semantics). https://epub.uni-bayreuth.de/881/1/Pakia.pdf
